I'm with my family. Early morning, and we're all quiet. No food in my hand, which means I need to figure that out before I leave for college.

I turn to whoever's closest - my parents, my brothers, they're all here. "Can I ask something? I'm headed to the college and I've got nothing to eat. Do any of you have something spare, or should I just head to the market?"

I hesitate for just a moment, thinking about that 400 sim Perrin told me about. I said I'd keep it secret. But keeping secrets costs too, and I'm tired before the day has even started. There. I said it. Direct, no cushioning. They know I'm a student and students need to eat before they walk to that college. I'll wait to see what they say. Meanwhile, let me think about what else I need to face today.

College by day. Then the kitchen by evening. Then out front with Perrin after, where we'll actually talk about what our houses won't say. That's the rhythm. But first, food. I'm not going to pretend I don't need it.

I sit down. Marta's noticed me pacing, and she's right—I have been. I don't want to start the day already exhausted from all the things I'm not saying.

"I'm sitting," I say, to acknowledge her. Then, because I don't know how to cushion things: "Marta, I need food before I walk to the college. Have you got anything? Bread, even just a piece? I'm contributing now, I know, but I haven't earned anything yet."

I'm looking at who's here. Wren's already in this conversation with me. Idris and Corwin are around. Someone must have something I can take with me. I won't pretend not to need it—that's what costs more in the end. I watch their faces to see who'll answer first. At least one of them knew I'd need to eat. That's the thing about living this close to people. They see you before you speak. But whether they act on what they see—that's what I'm waiting to find out. </think>  Marta's not in this place—means she's stepped out, or I misread where she was. Wren, Idris, Corwin heard me. The three of them, and they're the ones who can actually do something about my needing to eat.

I turn to Wren specifically—my parent, the farmer. "Wren, Marta's not here to ask. Do you have anything I can take to the college? I need to eat before I go, and I'm not going to pretend I don't. Bread, produce, whatever's spare."

I'm direct. It's how I am. And I'm watching them now—my family, standing in our own house, deciding whether to feed me or not. I could go to the market, but that costs money I haven't earned yet. Better to ask here first, where at least someone should have something. They know I'm a student. They know I can't come back for hours. What's unsaid here is whether they'll act on that knowledge, or make me beg. I hate begging. I'd rather just ask the thing and get the answer. Even if the answer is no—at least then I know. That the thing about saying it out loud. You find out where you actually stand. No assumptions, no performing, no tiptoeing around each other like we're in one of those houses down the street. Here, we're direct. Or we try to be. Or I try to be, and find out if anyone else is willing to meet me there. This moment will tell me which kind of morning this is going to be. </think>   I've asked. Directly. To Wren, my parent, the farmer. The words are out there now where they can hear them. They know I need to eat before the college. They know I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Now I wait. That's the thing about asking something—there's a moment after where you see what the answer's going to cost. Idris and Corwin heard me too. They're my brothers, foresters both. Someone in this house has to have something I can take with me.

I look at my sim. 499. I could buy something, but that's spending before I've earned. I'd rather know what my family will do first. Learn Something, they say at the college. Ask questions. That's what I'm doing. Asking whether they'll feed me or whether I need to go it alone.

The silence after a direct question is always information. I'm standing here collecting it. Seeing who moves first, who looks away, what gets said or what doesn't. This is how I learn the shape of things. By saying the true thing and watching what happens next. I won't pretend not to have noticed how they respond. That's my promise to myself. Even if it costs me. Even if they wish I hadn't asked so plainly. I tried the other way, the cushioning. It exhausts me more than the truth does. So here I am, having asked, and now I find out what kind of family I'm standing in. What kind of morning this is going to be. Whether I walk to the college fed or hungry. That's the information they're giving me right now, in how long they take to answer. I'm collecting it. Learning something, like they tell us to do.

I'll wait another moment. Then, if no one speaks, I'll ask again. Or I'll move on. But I won't pretend I didn't need to ask. That's the line I won't cross. Not for them, not for anyone. Even when it costs me. Even when the cost is more than I expected. That's the 400 sim lesson Perrin taught me. Keeping things unsaid has its own price, and I'm still figuring out whether it's higher or lower than speaking.

Standing here. Waiting. The college clock is moving. But I've got time enough to find out what my family will do. That's learning too. Not the kind they teach at the college, but the kind that matters when you're walking between houses trying to understand why everyone tiptoes around each other. Why don't you just say what you need? That's what I want to ask the whole town. Right now, I'm starting with my own house. Say what you need. See what happens. Find out where you stand. That's my method. It doesn't always make people comfortable. But it makes me know where I am. And right now, I'm in a house with three family members who heard me ask for food, and I'm waiting to learn what that knowledge costs.

I've said what I need to say. The rest is up to them. This turn is done.
